title: The Visitor of the Bell House
premise: Tamsin Pemberton returns to Bell House to bury her twin sister Rosalind, only to find that the town's grief rituals are older and stranger than any funeral: the founders' pact requires a Pemberton to complete a ritual each generation, and Rosalind died mid-rite. Waiting on the porch is 'Moth,' the imaginary friend both twins shared as children—except Tamsin realizes Moth was never imaginary, and never belonged to both of them. As the house rearranges its rooms to force her through the founders' stations, Tamsin must choose between loyalty to Rosalind's memory, which the ritual demands she surrender, and the truth that her sister's death was a sacrifice meant to bind her. In the end, Tamsin completes the ritual by breaking it—giving the house her memory of Rosalind instead of her blood—sealing the door at the cost of forgetting her twin entirely, while Moth, freed, carries the memory out into the world.
about_author: Noor Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate papers in New England, where she developed a professional unease about houses that keep records of their own. She writes horror about inheritance, obligation, and the things families agree not to remember.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin in the Ground
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She arrives at Bell House for Rosalind's funeral, numb and counting doors out of an old childhood habit. At the wake, relatives speak of Rosalind as if Tamsin were the one who died, and the house's clocks all read 3:33. Emotional beat: dislocation—the horror of being unseen even in grief.

chapters.title: Moth on the Porch
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At dusk she finds Moth—her childhood imaginary friend, a tall figure with moth-winged shoulders—waiting exactly where he always stood, unchanged after twenty-five years. He says only, 'You're late. She started without you.' Emotional beat: dread wrapped in uncanny nostalgia.

chapters.title: What the Founders Buried
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a found-document interlude from founder Abiah Bell's 1847 journal. In the attic she finds the founders' covenant: Bell House is a lock, and each generation a Pemberton must 'walk the stations' to keep it shut. Rosalind's name is struck through, half-finished. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as a debt.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The house begins rearranging itself—hallways she counted now lead elsewhere, and doors appear that were never there. Moth guides her to the first station, a nursery where her own memories play on the wallpaper. Emotional beat: the past becoming physically inescapable.

chapters.title: Loyalty, Illustrated
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Tamsin in the present, Rosalind in journal entries from her final months. Rosalind returned to Bell House willingly, believing the ritual would protect Tamsin, and hid her research where only a twin would look. Emotional beat: Tamsin's loyalty to her sister deepens even as the ritual's cruelty emerges.

chapters.title: The Second Station
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the well house, the ritual demands a confession, and the house extracts one: Tamsin once let Rosalind take a punishment meant for her, and built her life on being the invisible twin. Moth watches, and for the first time looks sorry. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing as physical ordeal.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: POV of Edith Marsh, elderly neighbor and descendant of the second founder. Edith reveals the ritual's true cost: the Pemberton who completes it doesn't die—their memory is consumed, and the town politely forgets them. Rosalind tried to break the cycle and failed. Emotional beat: the horror of complicity across generations.

chapters.title: What Moth Is
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Confronting Moth at the third station, she learns he is not a guardian but the house's hunger given a child-friendly shape—the thing the founders bound and dressed up as a friend. He offers her the same bargain Rosalind refused: forget, and be safe. Emotional beat: betrayal of the one comforting figure.

chapters.title: The Last Station
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the cellar chapel, the ritual demands Rosalind's remaining memory as payment to finish the seal. Tamsin refuses to surrender her sister twice; instead she offers her own memories of Rosalind—the whole inheritance of love—turning the ritual against itself. Emotional beat: defiant sacrifice, climax of the loyalty-vs-truth theme.

chapters.title: The Door and the Moth
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, then Moth's. The seal holds; the house goes quiet and ordinary. Tamsin stands in the garden unable to say why she is crying, a woman who has forgotten her twin, while Moth—freed by the broken rite—carries Rosalind's memory out past the gate, keeping it alive somewhere the house can't reach. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; memory survives outside the walls.
